1. Random seed¶

1.1. Fixing the seed makes the random splits, random searches and permutations reproducible. This also makes comparisons fair because models see the same data. It does not guarantee identical results across all software versions or prove that a model works for every possible split.

2. Dataset¶

2.1. There are 17,379 materials (rows).

2.2. The input has 342 floating point columns and one text identifier column (MOFname). Depending on the pandas version, text may appear as object or str. The 164 selected descriptors and the regression target are numerical. The binary column added below is integer valued. Identifiers and other adsorption outputs are excluded from the predictors.

3. Stratification¶

3.1. Stratifying preserves approximately the same proportions of low and high uptake materials in each split. Without it, a small set could contain too few high performers, making training less representative or evaluation unstable. Stratification on two bins does not guarantee identical distributions within each bin.

4. Binary target¶

4.1. A material is high performing if its CO₂ uptake is strictly greater than 15 mmol/g, following the starter's example. This label is used only for splitting; we still predict continuous uptake.

5. Train/test split¶

5.1. We use 80% for the training pool and 20% for testing. A single test point would give a very unreliable error estimate. Too few training points usually reduce model quality. For a very small dataset We would prefer cross-validation and retain as much training data as possible; for a huge dataset even a small test fraction may give enough test examples. More test than training points is possible, but often wastes useful training information.

Exact KRR stores an n × n kernel and its fitting cost grows roughly as n³. We therefore take a stratified random sample of 1,500 materials from the training pool only for every fit and search, as explicitly permitted in the starter notebook. This leaves 13,903 materials in the training pool, of which 1,500 are used for fitting, and 3,476 independent test materials. All comparisons use the same fitted training subset. We do not use the unused training rows to report test performance.

5.2. The held-out test set estimates prediction errors for unseen materials drawn from a similar population. Training errors alone are optimistic.

5.3. Hyperparameters are selected by cross-validation within training data. Repeatedly selecting models using the test error would leak information and give an optimistic estimate. The educational test comparisons below do not determine the chosen model.

In [5]:
df_train_pool, df_test = train_test_split(
    df, train_size=0.8, test_size=0.2, random_state=RANDOM_SEED,
    stratify=df[TARGET_BINARY])
df_train, df_unused = train_test_split(
    df_train_pool, train_size=1500, random_state=RANDOM_SEED,
    stratify=df_train_pool[TARGET_BINARY])
X_train, y_train = df_train[FEATURES], df_train[TARGET]
X_test, y_test = df_test[FEATURES], df_test[TARGET]
assert set(df_train.index).isdisjoint(df_test.index)
display(pd.DataFrame({name: {'n': len(part), 'high uptake fraction': part[TARGET_BINARY].mean()}
    for name, part in [('full data', df), ('training pool', df_train_pool),
                       ('fitted training subset', df_train), ('test', df_test)]}).T)
# Same five stratified folds for every search, stratifying only to balance uptake bins.
cv = list(StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_SEED).split(
    X_train, df_train[TARGET_BINARY]))

6. Correlations (including bonus)¶

6.1. Pearson measures linear association between values. Spearman is Pearson correlation between ranks and measures monotonic association, including nonlinear trends. Neither proves causation. Constant features have undefined correlations and are omitted from the rankings. EDA uses training data only.

In [6]:
def target_correlations(target):
    nonconstant = X_train.loc[:, X_train.nunique() > 1]
    return pd.DataFrame({method: nonconstant.corrwith(df_train[target], method=method)
                         for method in ['pearson', 'spearman']})
corr_co2 = target_correlations(TARGET)
for method in ['pearson', 'spearman']:
    print('CO2: strongest absolute', method, 'correlations')
    display(corr_co2.loc[corr_co2[method].abs().nlargest(5).index].round(3))
plot_features = ['total_POV_gravimetric', 'density [g/cm^3]', 'Di', 'total_SA_gravimetric']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 7))
for ax, feature in zip(axes.flat, plot_features):
    ax.scatter(X_train[feature], y_train, s=7, alpha=.35)
    ax.set(xlabel=feature, ylabel='CO₂ uptake (mmol/g)',
           title=f"Pearson {corr_co2.loc[feature, 'pearson']:.2f}; Spearman {corr_co2.loc[feature, 'spearman']:.2f}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
CH4_TARGET = 'pure_uptake_methane_298.00_6500000'
corr_ch4 = target_correlations(CH4_TARGET)
print('Bonus: CH4 at 298 K and 65 bar; strongest Pearson correlations')
display(corr_ch4.loc[corr_ch4.pearson.abs().nlargest(5).index].round(3))
display(corr_co2.loc[plot_features].add_prefix('CO2_').join(corr_ch4.loc[plot_features].add_prefix('CH4_')).round(3))

6.2. The strongest Pearson correlation is with gravimetric surface area (0.922), followed by volumetric pore volume (0.917). Density has a strong negative correlation (-0.875). The strongest Spearman correlation is with gravimetric pore volume (0.956), suggesting a strong monotonic relationship that is less linear (Pearson 0.751). We expect pore volume and gravimetric surface area to correlate positively with high-pressure uptake, and density to often correlate negatively: more accessible pore space per gram can hold more gas.

6.3. Correlated features contain redundant information. They can make coefficients or feature importance unstable and obscure which descriptor is responsible for a prediction. In a distance-based kernel they can also give repeated weight to similar information.

6.4. The comparison uses the same training rows. For CH4, gravimetric surface area has Pearson 0.971 and gravimetric pore volume 0.919, compared with 0.922 and 0.751 for CO2. Thus both remain important, but their linear associations are stronger here for CH4. Geometry should matter for both at these relatively high pressures, but the coefficients need not match. CO₂ and CH₄ have different interactions and molecular properties; these columns also correspond to different pressures (16 versus 65 bar), so differences cannot be attributed to gas identity alone.

7. Dummy estimator API¶

7.1. Mean and median DummyRegressors do not learn relationships from X, their fitted constants depend only on y. X remains in the common estimator API so the dummy can replace another regressor in a pipeline; prediction uses its number of rows to determine how many constant predictions to return.

8. Fit the baselines¶

8.1–8.2. Both baselines are fitted below on the same training subset.

In [7]:
dummyregressor_mean = DummyRegressor(strategy='mean').fit(X_train, y_train)
dummyregressor_median = DummyRegressor(strategy='median').fit(X_train, y_train)
models = {'Dummy mean': dummyregressor_mean, 'Dummy median': dummyregressor_median}
def get_regression_metrics(model, X, y_true):
    pred = model.predict(X)
    return {'MAE': mean_absolute_error(y_true, pred),
            'MSE': mean_squared_error(y_true, pred),
            'max_error': max_error(y_true, pred)}
def metrics_table(selected):
    rows = []
    for name, model in selected.items():
        for split, X, y in [('train', X_train, y_train), ('test', X_test, y_test)]:
            rows.append({'model': name, 'split': split, **get_regression_metrics(model, X, y)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(['model', 'split'])
def plot_evaluation(model, name):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 6))
    for row, (split, X, y) in enumerate([('train', X_train, y_train), ('test', X_test, y_test)]):
        pred = model.predict(X)
        error = np.asarray(y) - pred
        lo, hi = min(y.min(), pred.min()), max(y.max(), pred.max())
        axes[row, 0].scatter(y, pred, s=6, alpha=.3)
        axes[row, 0].plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], 'k--')
        axes[row, 0].set(xlabel='True uptake (mmol/g)', ylabel='Predicted uptake (mmol/g)', title=split+' parity')
        axes[row, 1].hist(error, bins=35)
        axes[row, 1].set(xlabel='True − predicted (mmol/g)', ylabel='Count', title=split+' errors')
        axes[row, 2].scatter(y, error, s=6, alpha=.3)
        axes[row, 2].axhline(0, color='k', linestyle='--')
        axes[row, 2].set(xlabel='True uptake (mmol/g)', ylabel='True − predicted (mmol/g)', title=split+' residuals')
    fig.suptitle(name); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
display(metrics_table(models).round(3))

9. Baseline errors¶

9.1. The table gives maximum absolute error, MAE and MSE for both sets. MAE and maximum error have units mmol/g; MSE has units (mmol/g)². The mean minimizes training MSE among constant predictions, and the median minimizes training MAE. Baseline MSE is therefore expected to be roughly the target variance for the mean model; the worst error depends on the most extreme uptake.

9.2. The measured values fit these expectations: training MAE is 6.324 for the median versus 6.405 for the mean, while training MSE is lower for the mean (55.014 versus 57.388). Test MAEs are similar, 6.160 and 6.230 mmol/g. This does not surprise us because both models only learn one constant. A large maximum error is compatible with a moderate MAE because a few extreme cases can be much worse than a typical point.

9.3. A metric needs context: compare against baselines on the same split and report several metrics. A complex model is only useful if it improves on simple predictions for the intended application.

10. Unscaled KRR¶

10.1. KRR can learn nonlinear relationships and could beat the baselines, but the default RBF kernel can fail badly on unscaled features. Large numerical differences can make similarities between different materials almost zero.

In [8]:
krr = KernelRidge(kernel='rbf').fit(X_train, y_train)
models['Raw KRR'] = krr
display(metrics_table(models).round(3))
print('Training kernel shape:', (len(X_train), len(X_train)))
print('Dual weights shape:', krr.dual_coef_.shape)
print('Test-to-training kernel shape:', (len(X_test), len(X_train)))

10.2. Raw KRR has training MAE 5.868 but test MAE 11.725 mmol/g, worse than the mean baseline (6.230). Its test MSE is 189.915 versus 52.376 for the mean baseline. The raw feature scales make the default kernel ineffective for unseen materials; the lower training error does not establish useful prediction.

10.3. With n = 1,500 training materials, K is 1,500 × 1,500 and the dual coefficient vector is length 1,500. Prediction uses a test-to-training kernel of shape 3,476 × 1,500.

11. Parity plots and errors¶

11.1–11.2. A perfect prediction lies on the dashed diagonal. Errors are defined as true minus predicted, so positive errors mean underprediction.

In [9]:
for name, model in models.items():
    plot_evaluation(model, name)

11.3. We would not tolerate the raw KRR errors for screening millions of materials. Its test MAE is 11.725 mmol/g and its maximum error is 32.749 mmol/g, so the error can be comparable to the uptake itself. It can strongly underpredict high-uptake materials and discard promising candidates. A screening model should retain high performers even if some less promising candidates are also selected. The improved model is assessed later; selected candidates would still need confirmation by simulations or experiments.

11.4. The dummy models give horizontal parity bands at the training mean or median. The raw KRR fits training points better, but its test predictions cluster close to zero rather than following the diagonal. Its test residuals therefore increase with true uptake, showing systematic underprediction. This explains why raw KRR performs worse than the baselines. The same plotting function is used for every subsequent fitted model.

12. Why scale?¶

12.1. The RBF kernel uses squared distances. A descriptor with a large numerical range can dominate these distances even if it is not physically more important. Standard scaling centers each feature and divides by its training standard deviation. Fitting the scaler inside each CV fold prevents information from the validation fold from affecting preprocessing.

13. Scaled pipeline¶

13.1–13.3. StandardScaler is followed by RBF KRR; both are fitted using training data only.

The scaled model reduces test MAE to 1.593 mmol/g, compared with 11.725 for raw KRR. Its test MSE is 6.463 (mmol/g)^2 and maximum error is 21.349 mmol/g. Scaling helps substantially, although some large errors remain.

In [10]:
pipe_w_scaling = Pipeline([('scaling', StandardScaler()), ('krr', KernelRidge(kernel='rbf'))])
pipe_w_scaling.fit(X_train, y_train)
models['Scaled KRR'] = pipe_w_scaling
display(metrics_table({'Scaled KRR': pipe_w_scaling}).round(3))
plot_evaluation(pipe_w_scaling, 'Scaled KRR')

14. Hyperparameter tuning (including random-search bonus)¶

14.1–14.2. We tune regularization α, RBF γ and the scaler. Larger γ gives a narrower kernel. We use logarithmic grids because the useful scales are not known in advance. StandardScaler and MinMaxScaler are compared; a step could also be disabled with None.

14.3. Five-fold CV trains on four folds and validates on the fifth, rotating through all five. The mean validation MAE selects the model, which is then refitted on all 1,500 training materials. A coarse search is followed by one local refinement. The refinement does not improve the best CV MAE (1.0433 mmol/g), so we stop. The selected parameters are StandardScaler, alpha = 0.001 and gamma = 0.001. The search is deliberately finite; it cannot prove a global optimum. All model selection uses validation scores, not test errors.

14.4. Validation results may guide parameter choices; the test set estimates performance after those choices are fixed. Reusing test errors for selection would make this estimate optimistic.

14.5. After refitting, training MAE is 0.640 mmol/g, MSE is 0.988 (mmol/g)^2 and maximum error is 6.531 mmol/g. Test MAE is 1.036 mmol/g, MSE is 2.510 (mmol/g)^2 and maximum error is 10.436 mmol/g. The higher test errors show a generalization gap, but the tuned model improves substantially on both baselines. The test plots are closer to the diagonal, while the maximum error shows that individual predictions can still be inaccurate.

In [11]:
param_grid = {'scaling': [StandardScaler(), MinMaxScaler()],
              'krr__alpha': [0.001, 0.03, 1.0],
              'krr__gamma': [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01]}
def run_search(search):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print('Best parameters:', search.best_params_)
    print(f'Best CV MAE: {-search.best_score_:.4f}; elapsed: {elapsed:.1f} s')
    return elapsed
grid_krr = GridSearchCV(pipe_w_scaling, param_grid, cv=cv, scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error', n_jobs=1)
grid_time = run_search(grid_krr)
best = grid_krr.best_params_
refined_grid = {'scaling': [clone(best['scaling'])],
                'krr__alpha': [best['krr__alpha'] / 3, best['krr__alpha'], best['krr__alpha'] * 3],
                'krr__gamma': [best['krr__gamma'] / 3, best['krr__gamma'], best['krr__gamma'] * 3]}
refined_krr = GridSearchCV(pipe_w_scaling, refined_grid, cv=cv, scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error', n_jobs=1)
run_search(refined_krr)
tuned_search = max([grid_krr, refined_krr], key=lambda search: search.best_score_)
models['Tuned KRR'] = tuned_search.best_estimator_
print('14.5: tuned model errors')
display(metrics_table({'Tuned KRR': models['Tuned KRR']}).round(3))
plot_evaluation(models['Tuned KRR'], 'Tuned KRR')

14.6. In this run random search found the same best parameters and CV MAE (1.0433 mmol/g) as the coarse grid while evaluating 6 rather than 18 candidates. The table gives the measured runtimes on exactly the same coarse grid. Random search evaluates fewer candidates and can find a competitive solution more cheaply, but may miss the best grid point. The outcome depends on the draw and search space; this single comparison does not show that random search is always better.

15. Low-variance features¶

15.1. A constant feature cannot distinguish materials. Removing constant or nearly constant descriptors reduces redundant dimensions and may reduce noise and cost.

15.2. Small variance does not imply no predictive information: a rare functional group might be important. A raw variance cutoff depends on units, so it can unfairly remove small-scale descriptors. Applying it after standard scaling would also defeat its purpose for nonconstant features because their variances become approximately one.

16. Variance threshold and random search¶

16.1–16.2. Selection is fitted before scaling, inside the pipeline and each CV fold. We compare zero (constants only) with a small raw variance threshold; the latter is an exploratory choice with the units limitation above.

The search selects a zero variance threshold, retaining 138 of 164 descriptors (26 constants are removed). Its CV MAE is 1.0635 mmol/g. Test MAE is 1.058 mmol/g, MSE is 2.523 (mmol/g)^2 and maximum error is 11.186 mmol/g. This search does not improve on the tuned KRR, so removing constants is useful for reducing the input size but does not guarantee better predictions.

In [13]:
pipe_variance_threshold = Pipeline([
    ('variance_threshold', VarianceThreshold()),
    ('scaling', StandardScaler()), ('krr', KernelRidge(kernel='rbf'))])
param_grid_variance_threshold = {

    'scaling': [StandardScaler(), MinMaxScaler()],
    'krr__alpha': refined_grid['krr__alpha'],
    'krr__gamma': refined_grid['krr__gamma']}
random_variance_threshold = RandomizedSearchCV(pipe_variance_threshold,
    param_grid_variance_threshold, n_iter=12, cv=cv, scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error',
    random_state=RANDOM_SEED, n_jobs=1)
run_search(random_variance_threshold)
models['Variance-selection KRR'] = random_variance_threshold.best_estimator_
print('Retained descriptors:', models['Variance-selection KRR'].named_steps['variance_threshold'].get_support().sum())
display(metrics_table({'Variance-selection KRR': models['Variance-selection KRR']}).round(3))
plot_evaluation(models['Variance-selection KRR'], 'Variance-selection KRR')

17. Bonus: alternative feature selection¶

17.1. We use SelectKBest with a univariate regression F-score, which is suitable for a continuous target. LinearSVC from the suggested example is a classifier and would require classification labels. Constant columns are removed first. Selection remains inside CV so it cannot see validation targets. Univariate selection can miss useful interactions and select redundant descriptors.

The selected pipeline retains 50 descriptors and has CV MAE 1.0441 mmol/g. Its test MAE is 1.025 mmol/g. Although this particular test error is slightly lower, its CV MAE is slightly higher than the tuned KRR's 1.0433 mmol/g. We therefore retain the tuned KRR as the final model, following the validation criterion rather than choosing from test results.

In [14]:
pipe_selection = Pipeline([('constants', VarianceThreshold()),
    ('feature_selection', SelectKBest(score_func=f_regression)),
    ('scaling', StandardScaler()), ('krr', KernelRidge(kernel='rbf'))])
selection_params = {'feature_selection__k': [20, 50, 'all'],
                    'krr__alpha': refined_grid['krr__alpha'],
                    'krr__gamma': refined_grid['krr__gamma']}
selection_search = RandomizedSearchCV(pipe_selection, selection_params, n_iter=6, cv=cv,
    scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error', random_state=RANDOM_SEED, n_jobs=1)
run_search(selection_search)
models['Univariate-selection KRR'] = selection_search.best_estimator_
display(metrics_table({'Univariate-selection KRR': models['Univariate-selection KRR']}).round(3))
plot_evaluation(models['Univariate-selection KRR'], 'Univariate-selection KRR')

19. Effect of regularization¶

19.1. Writing the dual coefficients as c, kernel ridge regression minimizes

$$\|\mathbf y-K\mathbf c\|_2^2+\alpha\,\mathbf c^T K\mathbf c,\qquad \mathbf c=(K+\alpha I)^{-1}\mathbf y.$$

This corresponds to penalizing the squared norm of the fitted function in kernel space. Very small α weakens regularization: fitting the training data becomes easier, but noise, unstable solutions and overfitting become more likely. Large α shrinks the coefficients and can cause underfitting. Without target centering or a separate intercept, predictions approach zero as α becomes extremely large. Small α does not guarantee worse test performance; the result also depends on γ and the data.

Following the starter notebook, We fix α to each extreme, re-optimize γ using training CV, and evaluate the refitted models. This is a diagnostic exercise after the final model choice; it does not change that choice. With alpha = 1e-10, training MAE is almost zero but test MAE is 1.838 mmol/g, consistent with overfitting. With alpha = 1e6, test MAE is 11.719 mmol/g, consistent with severe underfitting.

In [16]:
alpha_rows = []
for alpha in [1e-10, 1e6]:

        {'krr__alpha': [alpha], 'krr__gamma': [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1]},
        cv=cv, scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error', n_jobs=1)
    run_search(search)
    name = f'Alpha = {alpha:g}'
    models[name] = search.best_estimator_
    alpha_rows.append({'alpha': alpha, 'gamma': search.best_params_['krr__gamma'], 'CV MAE': -search.best_score_})
    display(metrics_table({name: models[name]}).round(3))
    plot_evaluation(models[name], name)

20. Pressure and physical interpretation¶

20.1. At low pressure, uptake depends strongly on affinity for the first adsorption sites, so chemical descriptors such as RACs may be particularly informative. At high pressure, available pore volume and accessible surface area become more important because the pores are filling. Both geometry and chemistry can matter at either pressure; this is an expected trend rather than a universal rule.

21. Complete permutation importance¶

21.1. Shuffle one feature column, predict again, and record the score. Permutation breaks its relationship with the target while preserving its distribution. Importance is baseline score minus shuffled score. With negative MAE scoring, positive importance is the increase in MAE after shuffling, in mmol/g.

In [17]:
def _calculate_permutation_scores(estimator, X, y, col_idx, random_state, n_repeats, scorer):
    random_state = check_random_state(random_state)
    X_permuted = X.copy()
    scores = np.zeros(n_repeats)
    shuffling_idx = np.arange(X.shape[0])
    for n_round in range(n_repeats):
        random_state.shuffle(shuffling_idx)
        if hasattr(X_permuted, 'iloc'):
            col = X_permuted.iloc[shuffling_idx, col_idx].copy()
            col.index = X_permuted.index
            X_permuted.iloc[:, col_idx] = col
        else:
            X_permuted[:, col_idx] = X_permuted[shuffling_idx, col_idx]
        scores[n_round] = scorer(estimator, X_permuted, y)
    return scores

def permutation_importance(estimator, X, y, scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error',
                           n_repeats=5, n_jobs=1, random_state=None):
    if not hasattr(X, 'iloc'):
        X = check_array(X, dtype=None)
    random_state = check_random_state(random_state)
    random_seed = random_state.randint(np.iinfo(np.int32).max + 1)
    scorer = check_scoring(estimator, scoring=scoring)
    baseline_score = scorer(estimator, X, y)
    scores = Parallel(n_jobs=n_jobs)(delayed(_calculate_permutation_scores)(
        estimator, X, y, col_idx, random_seed, n_repeats, scorer)
        for col_idx in range(X.shape[1]))
    importances = baseline_score - np.array(scores)
    return Bunch(importances_mean=importances.mean(axis=1),
                 importances_std=importances.std(axis=1), importances=importances)

# A small functional check against sklearn also covers the NumPy branch.
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance as sklearn_permutation_importance
check_X = X_train.iloc[:80, :3].to_numpy()
check_y = y_train.iloc[:80].to_numpy()
check_model = KernelRidge(kernel='rbf').fit(check_X, check_y)
own = permutation_importance(check_model, check_X, check_y, random_state=42)
reference = sklearn_permutation_importance(check_model, check_X, check_y,
    scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error', n_repeats=5, random_state=42)
np.testing.assert_allclose(own.importances, reference.importances)
print('NumPy implementation agrees with sklearn.')

NumPy implementation agrees with sklearn.

22. Five most important features¶

22.1. After model selection is frozen, We estimate permutation importance on a fixed stratified subset of 400 test rows to limit computation. It is used for interpretation only, not to retrain or select features. Five repeats provide a basic estimate of permutation variability; their standard deviation is not a confidence interval.

22.2. The five highest-ranked features are: total_SA_gravimetric, total_POV_volumetric, density [g/cm^3], total_POV_gravimetric, sum-f-lig-S-2.

Of these, 4 are pore-geometry descriptors. Geometry is expected to matter for high-pressure uptake because accessible space limits gas loading. Chemical RAC descriptors may also contribute through adsorption interactions and correlations with geometry. The exact ordering was not predictable in advance.

Correlated descriptors can share importance, so shuffling one may appear unimportant when another supplies similar information. Permutation can also create physically unrealistic feature combinations. These values describe this fitted model on these materials and do not establish causal importance.

The final comparison below contains every fitted model requested in the exercises. The saved model was chosen using CV, before the regularization diagnostic and permutation analysis.

Conclusion¶

Scaling the features and tuning the KRR model reduced the test MAE from 6.230 mmol/g for the mean baseline to 1.036 mmol/g. Pore geometry descriptors were especially important for predicting high-pressure CO2 uptake. Our model could help screen promising MOFs, but individual predictions still need confirmation.
